chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Ala' ibn Razin, from Musa ibn Bakr, from Zurara, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Ibn Umm Maktum called the Adhan for the morning prayer, and a man passed by the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) while he was eating the pre-dawn meal (suhoor). He invited him to eat with him, but he said, 'O Messenger of Allah, the Mu'adhdhin has called the Adhan for Fajr.' So he (peace be upon him and his family) said, said, 'This is Ibn Umm Maktum, and he calls the Adhan at night. When Bilal calls the Adhan, then at that time, refrain (from eating).'

key_terms.ابْنُ أُمِّ مَكْتُومٍ: Ibn Umm Maktum, a companion of the Prophet known for his blindness, who would call the Adhan early.
key_terms.بِلَيْلٍ: At night (referring to the early call).
key_terms.فَعِنْدَ ذَلِكَ: Then at that time (referring to the specific moment of Bilal's call).
key_terms.يَتَسَحَّرُ: He was eating the pre-dawn meal (suhoor).

ai.seo_question: When does the time for fasting begin according to the Adhan of Ibn Umm Maktum versus Bilal?
ai.summary: This hadith highlights the jurisprudential distinction between the 'false dawn' (Al-Fajr Al-Kadhib) and the 'true dawn' (Al-Fajr Al-Sadiq), a critical concept in Shia fiqh for determining the precise start of the fasting period. By instructing the companion to continue eating until Bilal’s call, the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) clarified that Ibn Umm Maktum’s early adhan, based on his individual perception, did not bind the community, thereby establishing the principle of following the public, verified time of true dawn.
